summary: As Mughal power collapsed in the 18th century, Sikh bands organised into misls fought the Afghan armies of Ahmad Shah Durrani and divided the Punjab among a confederacy of chiefs. Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl took Lahore in 1799, was crowned Maharaja in 1801 and united the Punjab, then conquered Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. After his death in 1839, court murders and an overmighty army weakened the state; two wars with the British East India Company followed, and the Punjab was annexed in 1849.
details: In 1748 the Sikh fighting bands of the Punjab were reorganised into misls under one army, the Dal Khalsa, commanded by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. They fought the Mughal governors and the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, who invaded India repeatedly. In 1762 Durrani's army caught a large Sikh force at Kup and killed thousands of people, a disaster remembered as the Vadda Ghallughara, the 'great massacre'. Yet the Sikhs recovered remarkably fast: about six months later they defeated the Afghans at Amritsar, and Durrani could not crush them.

Sirhind, between the Sutlej and the Yamuna, was held for Ahmad Shah Durrani as the key to the eastern Punjab. In 1764 the misls captured it, and the territory between Karnal and Ferozepur was divided among several misls and administered jointly. The Phulkian misl held much of this southern Malwa region, between Sirhind and Delhi, and its states later survived as the Cis-Sutlej states, outside Ranjit Singh's kingdom. The capture carried Sikh power towards Delhi and showed that Durrani could no longer hold the eastern Punjab.

Lahore, the old capital of the Punjab, changed hands several times during the Afghan wars; the Sikhs won a siege of the city in 1761 and began striking their own coins. From 1765 Lahore was ruled by a triumvirate of Sikh chiefs, and the Bhangi misl, the strongest power in the Majha region, came to dominate western Punjab, including Lahore and Amritsar. By the 1770s more than sixty Sikh-ruled principalities lay between the Yamuna and the Indus, many funded by the rakhi system of protection payments. The confederacy was powerful but divided.

Ranjit Singh, born in 1780, became chief of the Sukerchakia misl at the age of twelve when his father Maha Singh died in 1792. The Afghan ruler Zaman Shah Durrani invaded the Punjab in 1797–98 but soon retreated. On 7 July 1799 Ranjit Singh captured Lahore from the triumvirate that had held it since 1765, and Zaman Shah later recognised his hold on the city. Ranjit Singh moved his capital there from Gujranwala, founded by his grandfather Charat Singh. The capture made the Sukerchakias the leading misl and is counted as the beginning of the Sikh Empire.

On 12 April 1801 Ranjit Singh was formally crowned at Lahore by Sahib Singh Bedi, a descendant of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. The ceremony turned a misl chief into a sovereign Maharaja and marks the formal beginning of the Sikh Empire. He had already annexed the Jammu region in 1800. Over the following decade he absorbed the other misls one by one, building a single kingdom in the Punjab where there had been dozens of rival chiefs. Only the Phulkian and other chiefs south of the Sutlej stayed outside his rule.

Amritsar, home of the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple), was the spiritual centre of the Sikhs, and the Bhangi misl held it. In 1802, aged 22, Ranjit Singh took Amritsar from the Bhangis. Winning the holy city gave him great prestige among Sikhs. It also began his conquest of the remaining misls, which was largely complete by 1812: Kasur and Jhang were annexed in 1807, and by 1813 all the remaining misls had been absorbed. The Sikh Empire now covered the central Punjab, from the Sutlej towards the Indus.

As Ranjit Singh's power grew he looked across the Sutlej, where the Phulkian and other Sikh chiefs ruled and where his forces occupied Faridkot in 1807. There his ambitions ran into those of the British East India Company. In 1809 the two sides signed the Treaty of Amritsar, which set the Sutlej as the eastern boundary of Ranjit Singh's kingdom; he returned Faridkot to its ruler. The treaty kept peace with the British for more than thirty years and turned Ranjit Singh's expansion north and west, against the Afghans.

Attock, a fort guarding the crossing of the Indus, was held by the Afghan Durrani kingdom. In 1813 Ranjit Singh's general Mohkam Chand defeated the Afghan army in the Battle of Attock and captured the fort. It gave the Sikhs a strong point on the Indus and a gateway towards Peshawar and the north-west. The same year the last independent misls were annexed, so the Sikh kingdom now stretched across the Punjab from the Sutlej to the Indus, and the stage was set for war with the Afghans over Multan and Kashmir.

Multan, an ancient walled city in the southern Punjab, had been held by the Bhangi misl until the Afghan Durranis took it back in 1780. Since then it had been ruled by Afghan governors. In 1818 Ranjit Singh's son Kharak Singh and the general Misr Diwan Chand captured the city, ending Afghan influence east of the Indus. Multan gave the empire a large new province reaching towards the borders of Sindh, and its fall freed the Sikh army for a campaign against Kashmir the following year.

The Kashmir Valley was still ruled by governors of the Afghan Durrani kingdom. In 1819 a Sikh army defeated the Afghans at the Battle of Shopian, and Kashmir was annexed to the Sikh Empire. The same year the Namgyal kings of Ladakh, further east, began paying annual tribute to Lahore. In 1820 Ranjit Singh confirmed the Dogra Gulab Singh in his family's estates at Jammu, and the Dogras became powerful vassals in the hills. Kashmir remained one of the empire's most valuable provinces until it was lost in 1846.

Ranjit Singh pushed west into Pashtun country. After the Battle of Nowshera in 1823, Peshawar paid tribute to Lahore, and in 1834 the Sikhs took the city from the Peshawar Sardars and formally annexed it. In the same year Zorawar Singh, general of Ranjit Singh's Dogra vassal Gulab Singh, conquered the Namgyal kingdom of Ladakh, and Baltistan was brought under Sikh suzerainty in 1839–40. The empire now reached from the Khyber Pass in the west to Ladakh in the Himalaya, and from the Sutlej to the borders of Sindh.

The Afghan emir Dost Mohammad Khan never accepted the loss of Peshawar. While many of the best Sikh troops were at a royal wedding in Lahore, he sent his son Wazir Akbar Khan with a large army against the Sikh fort at Jamrud, at the mouth of the Khyber Pass. In the battle on 30 April 1837 the Sikh commander Hari Singh Nalwa was mortally wounded, but the garrison held out until reinforcements arrived. Historians disagree over who won, but the Afghans withdrew, Peshawar stayed Sikh, and Jamrud was the last battle with the Afghans on the western frontier.

Ranjit Singh died in his sleep at Lahore on 27 June 1839. He left a large, well-trained army, built with the help of European officers such as Jean-François Allard and Jean-Baptiste Ventura, but no strong successor. His son Kharak Singh, his grandson Nau Nihal Singh, the regent Chand Kaur and Sher Singh followed one another within a few years, each killed or removed amid court intrigue. In 1843 the child Duleep Singh became Maharaja with his mother Jind Kaur as regent, while the army, which grew to over 80,000 men by 1845, became ever more powerful.

Tension with the British grew as both sides massed troops on the Sutlej. On 11 December 1845 the Sikh army crossed the river, and the British declared war. Led by the vizier Lal Singh and the commander Tej Singh, whom Sikh historians accuse of treachery, the Sikhs lost at Mudki, Ferozeshah and Aliwal. On 10 February 1846, at Sobraon, their bridge broke and thousands died. The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) took the Jullundur Doab and, in place of an indemnity, Kashmir and Hazara; the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh. By December a British resident effectively governed the rest of the kingdom.

In April 1848 two British officials, Vans Agnew and Anderson, were attacked at Multan and murdered on 19 April. The governor, Diwan Mulraj, was pulled into open rebellion, and the rising spread: Chattar Singh Attariwala rebelled in Hazara in August, and in September his son Sher Singh's army joined the revolt. The Sikhs fought the British at Ramnagar in November and at Chillianwala in January 1849, but were decisively beaten at Gujrat on 21 February 1849. At the end of March 1849 the young Duleep Singh was deposed and the Punjab was annexed by the East India Company.
